metadata.title: Why a 50-turn agent pays for the same screenshot 35 times unless it caches the pixels
metadata.purpose: NikBearBrown / Teardown cut. Same facts as the source hai-simple reel — a 50-turn computer-use agent that revisits the same five desktop states pays 100,000 image tokens instead of 10,000, because the API is stateless and re-tokenizes every screenshot from scratch. The fix is one field: cache_control={"type":"ephemeral"} on the first send turns later identical hashes into cache hits. Teardown voice explains the machinery (why stateless), reveals the design trade-off (identical-picture memoization, not similarity matching), and names the failure mode (a shifted cursor is a new hash — full price).
metadata.clock: narration (Kokoro am_onyx) — master clock; conform each beat to measured audio
metadata.prerequisites: tokens, LLM API calls, caching semantics
metadata.exclusions: full caching protocol, cache eviction policies

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. It looks like a bandwidth problem — the same image going down the wire fifty times. It isn't. The wire doesn't care. The tokenizer does: every screenshot is re-read from scratch, whether Claude has seen it or not. So why does a 50-turn agent pay to process the same picture over and over?

props.text:
Why does a 50-turn
agent waste bandwidth
resending the same
screenshot?

beats.narration_text: Take the machinery apart. A 50-turn form-filling task only ever shows five unique desktop states — the same handful of screens, appearing and reappearing. Do the naive math: 50 screenshots at 2,000 tokens each is 100,000 image tokens for a task that contains five actual pictures. The other 45 turns pay to re-tokenize things Claude already tokenized.

items.label: A 50-turn task shows only 5 unique desktop states
items.sub: The same handful of screens, appearing and reappearing across the run.

items.label: Naive: 50 × 2,000 = 100,000 tokens
items.sub: 100,000 image tokens spent on a task that contains five actual pictures.

beats.narration_text: The natural assumption is that the model already saw the screenshot once, so showing it again should be nearly free — it's already in the conversation, right there in context. That intuition comes from how humans read; you don't re-parse a sentence you just parsed. Here's where the intuition breaks.

items.label: The model already saw it once —
items.sub: The intuition: a screenshot in-context should be nearly free to reference again.

items.label: so showing it again should be nearly free
items.sub: That's how human reading works. It is not how the API works.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening under the hood. An API call has no memory between requests — that is the design choice. Every turn resends the entire conversation so far, images included, and the tokenizer runs across all of it from scratch, every single time. They optimized for stateless simplicity — no server-side sessions, no eviction bugs, nothing hidden — at the expense of paying to re-read what you already sent.

items.label: An API call has no memory between requests
items.sub: The design choice: stateless simplicity — no server-side session to go wrong.

items.label: Every turn resends everything, reprocessed from scratch
items.sub: The trade: you pay to re-tokenize what you already sent.

beats.narration_text: The fix is one field. Hash the screenshot, and mark it as cached the first time it's sent — cache_control set to type ephemeral. Now the server keeps the tokenized result under that hash. The next turn that ships the identical picture matches the hash and hits the cache instead of paying full price to reprocess. This works if you value stateless calls that opt into memory; it fails if you assumed the server remembers on its own.

items.label: Hash the screenshot, mark it cache_control: ephemeral
items.sub: One field, first send. The server stores the tokenized result under that hash.

items.label: The next identical hash hits the cache
items.sub: Same picture, same hash, nearly free — instead of full re-tokenization.

beats.narration_text: Back to the 50-turn task. Only the five unique states ever get tokenized in full — 2,000 tokens each, 10,000 total. The other 45 turns match hashes they've seen before, cache hits, nearly free. Ten thousand tokens instead of a hundred thousand. Same task, same screenshots, one flag.

items.label: 5 states tokenized in full: 10,000 total
items.sub: Only the five unique screens pay full price — 2,000 tokens apiece.

items.label: 10,000 instead of 100,000
items.sub: Same task, same screenshots — one flag turns 45 turns into cache hits.

beats.narration_text: Now the trade-off, honestly. This helps exactly when a screen repeats byte-for-byte — an idle dialog, a form nobody has touched. A cursor that moved a single pixel, or a field mid-type, is a different image, hashes to a different key, and pays full price again. The optimization is honest about what it is: identical-picture memoization, not similarity matching.

props.title: ONLY WHEN THE SCREEN REPEATS EXACTLY

items.label: Helps when a screen repeats byte-for-byte
items.sub: Idle dialogs, untouched forms — the same picture, hash for hash.

items.label: A moved cursor is a different hash — full price

beats.narration_text: And on the other side. This doesn't help a task that's genuinely novel every turn — a real navigation to a new page is a new state, tokenized like anything else. Caching can't invent savings where the screen actually changed; it can only stop billing you twice for the same picture. This works if you're doing repetitive computer use; it fails if every turn opens something new.

props.title: NOT WHEN THE SCREEN ACTUALLY CHANGES

items.label: Doesn't help a task that's novel every turn
items.sub: New page, new state, full tokenization — nothing to match.

items.label: Caching can't invent savings where the screen changed
items.sub: It stops double-billing repeats; it doesn't discount new pictures.

beats.narration_text: An unchanged screenshot isn't free just because the model already saw it — the API resends everything from scratch, every single turn. Marking it cached with one field is what turns a repeat picture into a near-zero-cost lookup.

props.quote: An unchanged screenshot isn't free just because the model already saw it — the API resends everything from scratch, every single turn. Marking it cached with one field is what turns a repeat picture into a near-zero-cost lookup.
props.sparkLine: Cache the pixels, not the memory.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste straight into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I'm building a 50-turn computer-use agent that revisits the same five desktop states repeatedly. Show me exactly where to place cache_control on the screenshot messages so each unique state is only billed once, and write the code that detects a repeated state and routes to the cached version instead of sending the raw image again. Go deeper: what happens when a screenshot changes by a single pixel, and how would you design a similarity-aware layer on top of exact-hash caching?

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm building a 50-turn computer-use agent with Claude's API. The task revisits the same 5 desktop states repeatedly, so ~45 of the 50 turns send a screenshot Claude has already seen. Right now every turn re-tokenizes the picture at ~2,000 tokens, so the run costs ~100,000 image tokens instead of the ~10,000 it should. Show me exactly where to place `cache_control={"type":"ephemeral"}` on the screenshot message blocks so each unique state is only billed once, and write the wrapper code that hashes each new screenshot, detects a repeated state, and routes it to the cached version instead of resending the raw image. Include the before/after token math and note what the code does NOT handle (e.g. near-duplicate screens).
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: what happens to the cache when a screenshot changes by a single pixel — and how would you design a similarity-aware caching layer on top of exact-hash caching so a moved cursor still hits?
